content: Rhabdomyosarcoma is the most common type of soft tissue sarcoma in children. Despite advances in treatment, the prognosis for patients with metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma has not significantly improved over the past few decades. High-dose chemotherapy (HDC) has been proposed as a potential treatment option to target minimal residual disease in patients with metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma. The purpose of this review was to evaluate whether HDC combined with stem cell rescue (SCR) is more effective than standard-dose chemotherapy in improving event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) in children and young adults with metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma. To gather evidence, the authors conducted a comprehensive search of databases, including MEDLINE (1966 to December 2009), EMBASE (1980 to December 2009), and CENTRAL (The Cochrane Library, Issue 1, 2009). They also manually reviewed reference lists of selected studies and conference proceedings from SIOP, ASPHO, and ASCO meetings held between 2000 and 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective or historical controlled clinical trials (CCTs) comparing HDC with SCR to conventional chemotherapy, and prospective case series involving at least 20 patients with newly diagnosed metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma. Two independent reviewers performed study selection, quality assessment, and data extraction. No randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were identified. The review included one prospective CCT, one retrospective CCT, and one non-controlled clinical trial. Additionally, another CCT was identified in abstract form from a conference proceeding. All included studies had significant methodological limitations, particularly the inability to rule out selection bias. One CCT reported that overall survival (OS) was significantly worse with HDC compared to oral maintenance therapy. However, in a subgroup of high-risk patients, no difference in survival outcomes was observed. The retrospective CCT found no significant difference in survival between HDC and conventional chemotherapy. The non-controlled clinical trial and the CCT reported in the conference proceeding showed survival outcomes similar to those reported in previous studies. Regarding toxicity, the data indicated that patients in the HDC group experienced higher rates of grade 3-4 toxicities. However, there was no difference in the number of toxic deaths between the HDC and conventional chemotherapy groups. The authors concluded that the current evidence does not support the use of HDC with SCR as a standard treatment for children with metastatic rhabdomyosarcoma. However, the studies included in the review were likely affected by significant bias, particularly selection bias, which may have underestimated the potential benefits of HDC. It is possible that the inclusion of a higher proportion of high-risk patients in the HDC arms contributed to the lack of observed benefit. To definitively determine whether HDC with SCR improves survival outcomes, a large, well-designed prospective randomized controlled trial is necessary.
